text: Hendrik Jacobus Scholten lived and worked in Teyler's fundatiehuis from 1863 until he died. He became art curator of the Teylers Stichting in 1872, and in 1904 he published a catalogue of the museum's collection. He also painted several pictures that hang in its galleries, along with decorations in the house itself. He followed Pieter de Hooch in his interior scenes. He taught Jacobus van Looy. Works by him hang in the Rijksmuseum too.

Henry Nelson O'Neil wrote a futuristic fantasy in which Britain in the year 3867 is a frozen wasteland excavated by an archaeologist from New Zealand. The book, Two Thousand Years Hence, let him voice his hostility to the Pre-Raphaelites and to the Reform Act. He was born in St. Petersburg. He belonged to The Clique, a group of artists that included Richard Dadd and William Powell Frith. His best known paintings deal with the Indian Mutiny, among them Eastward, Ho!, which shows British troops embarking for India.

Isabel Agnes Cowper was the first woman to hold the post of Official Museum Photographer at the South Kensington Museum, now the V&A. From 1868 until she retired in 1891 she made thousands of photographs of the museum, its loan objects and the construction of its buildings. Before that she was a wood engraver, trained with her siblings by their father. Henry Cole hired her and her sisters to engrave the illustrations for his guides to Westminster Abbey and Hampton Court Palace. She also cut the pictures for Ruskin's fairytale The King of the Golden River.

Jan Styka painted the Racławice Panorama together with Wojciech Kossak, a cyclorama 15 by 114 meters that is now shown in Wrocław. He was born in Lemberg, now Lviv, the son of a Czech officer, and studied in Vienna and then under Jan Matejko in Kraków. Later he moved to France. His Polonia was the centerpiece of Constitution Day celebrations in Lviv in 1891. He died in 1925 and was buried in Rome. In 1959 his remains were moved to Forest Lawn in the United States.

Gilles-Louis Chrétien played the cello and engraved. In 1787 he invented the physionotrace, a machine for taking portraits in profile from life. He worked at first with Edmé Quenedey and then with the miniaturist Jean-Baptiste Fouquet. Fouquet made the drawing and Chrétien engraved it in aquatint. Among the hundreds of sitters were Robespierre, Mirabeau and Marat. Dutch patriots who fled to France or visited Paris, such as Johan Valckenaer, ordered whole sets.

Fritz Petzholdt trained as a house painter before he entered the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts. There he studied under Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg. The year after he graduated he sold A Bog at Høsterkøb, with Peat Cutters, to the Royal Danish Painting Collection. He spent most of his artistic life in Italy, where he painted refined landscapes in a light palette. He died young, possibly by suicide.

Decker's family moved from Pest to Vienna in 1821, and he grew up in the imperial city. His father, Johann Stephan Decker, taught him to paint in watercolour and miniature. His brothers Albert and Gabriel were artists too. As early as 1835 he drew the composer Wenzel Müller. He taught painting in Vienna and was sometimes called Herr Professor. He was made a knight.

Gerrit Pietersz Sweelink painted a portrait of his brother, the organist Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck, who was known as the Orpheus of Amsterdam. According to Karel van Mander he learned first from the glass painter Jacob Lenartsz. He was such a good student that he was recommended to Cornelis van Haarlem. He lived in Antwerp for many years and in Rome for even longer, and in Italy he taught Pieter Lastman. He was born and died in Amsterdam. He is known for portraits and for mythological and religious pieces.

Hieronymus Francken II came from a large family of painters in Antwerp. His father, Frans Francken the Elder, gave him his first training, and his three brothers were painters too. With Frans II he helped develop new genres in Flemish art in the early 1600s. He painted religious scenes, portraits and fruit pieces. He also painted gallery interiors. His Connoisseurs at a Gallery is one of the gallery pictures.

Jacopino del Conte came from Florence and worked in both Florence and Rome. Like Cecchino del Salviati, he started out as an apprentice to Andrea del Sarto. His first frescoes were for the Oratory of San Giovanni Decollato in Rome, where the Preaching of Saint John the Baptist followed a drawing by Perin del Vaga. With Siciolante da Sermoneta he decorated the chapel of San Remigio in San Luigi dei Francesi. Later he painted the altarpiece Deposition for the oratory. He outlived Salviati by 35 years.

Jan Josef Horemans the Elder painted small anecdotal pictures in the tradition of 17th-century Flemish genre painters. His colours were rather dark. He first trained under the sculptor Michiel van der Voort the Elder and later under the painter Jan van Pee. In 1706 he became a master in the Antwerp Guild of St. Luke. The next year he married his first master's daughter, Maria Francisca. Their son Jan Josef the Younger also became a painter.

Franz Xaver Stöber learned engraving from his father and then at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. He was Austria's first steel engraver. In 1829 he was awarded a patent for a way of printing in color on steel or copper plates. From 1844 he taught engraving at the Academy. His output came to about 2,500 engravings, from full-sized portraits to book-sized vignettes. He was also an avid collector of early tin cans.

Fredrik Ahlstedt joined Victor Westerholm's artists' colony at Önningeby on the island of Åland in 1886, one of the first to do so. His wife Nina was a painter too, and the two kept returning there. He studied under Robert Wilhelm Ekman and then in Düsseldorf. He was prolific. He painted a wide range of portraits and landscapes. His work was shown in Stockholm in 1897 and in Paris in 1900.

Harlow paid Thomas Lawrence to let him into the studio and copy his pictures, and he stayed about eighteen months. They fell out after Harlow painted an inn signboard at Epsom in Lawrence's style and added Lawrence's initials. Friends nicknamed him Clarissa Harlowe because of his showy dress. He opposed the Royal Academy, yet he stood as a candidate and got only one vote, from Henry Fuseli. He first exhibited there in 1804.

Philippoteaux painted a cyclorama of the Siege of Paris during the Franco-Prussian War, one of his best-known works. A cyclorama is a large panorama on the inside of a cylinder, so a viewer standing in the middle is surrounded by the scene. He studied in the studio of Léon Cogniet and first showed at the Paris Salon in 1833. Later he made many works about the rise and successes of Napoleon, including a portrait of him in his regimental uniform. Mostly he is known as a battle painter.

Jacob Grimmer painted rural scenes and views around Antwerp. They moved Flemish landscape painting away from the world landscape, with its fantastic panoramas and gigantic rocks, toward greater simplicity. He was born in Antwerp, the son of a small merchant. Karel van Mander says he learned landscape painting first from Matthys Cock and later from Christian van den Queborn, but no written sources confirm it. His realistic colours made harmonic landscapes. His work influenced the next generation of Flemish landscape painters.

Copia, a French engraver, came from Landau, which was then part of France, and went on to Paris. He engraved a small portrait of Marie Antoinette after Piauger, which is very rare. He also engraved a head of Marat from a drawing that David made right after the assassination. His name is chiefly linked to Prud'hon, whose work he knew well. He died in Paris in 1799, too early to engrave Prud'hon's greatest works. His pupil Roger took up his manner.

James Henry Beard was the son of English and Scottish immigrants, and he grew up in Ohio after his family left Buffalo, where he was born. In Painesville he studied under Jarvis Frary Hanks. He started with watercolor and pastel, and portraits became his preferred genre. Henry Clay and John Quincy Adams were among his sitters. In 1846 he went back to New York to get his work noticed, and two years later the National Academy of Design took him in. He was elected a member in 1872.

Gabrielle-Marie Niel studied etching under Charles Méryon, after first lessons from Émile Wattier, a friend of her father's. She is chiefly noted for etchings of old Paris and other cities, along with pictures of Italy and Algeria. Her prints show Méryon's influence. She first exhibited at the Paris Salon in 1866. Alfred Cadart published her pictures of Paris and Algeria. The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco hold three of her etchings.

Jeanne-Philiberte Ledoux took lessons from Jean-Baptiste Greuze. In 1793 she showed three paintings at the Salon, among them Little Girls at a Crossroads and Concealed Love. She kept exhibiting there until 1819 and was a frequent exhibitor. She is known for miniatures and portraits. Only one work attributed to her is signed, and none are dated. She died in Belleville.

Krieghoff spent part of his boyhood in Schloss Mainberg, a 12th-century castle above the Main River, where his father helped set up a wallpaper factory. He moved to New York in 1836 and joined the US Army the next year, sketching the Second Seminole War. Around 1846 he settled in Montreal. There he befriended the Mohawks at Kahnawake and made oil paintings from his sketches of them. He lived in Quebec City from 1853 and painted many winter scenes, some in several variants. He is best known for Canadian genre scenes of landscape and outdoor life.

Eugene von Guérard toured Italy as a boy with his father, a miniature painter at the court of Emperor Francis I. In Rome he got to know German artists, among them the landscape painter Joseph Anton Koch. He then studied landscape painting at the Düsseldorf academy, where the aim was a truthful realism based on observation of nature. In 1852 he arrived in Victoria, Australia, determined to try his luck on the goldfields. He stayed in Australia until 1882. His finely detailed landscapes hang in the country's major galleries.

Johann Daniel Preissler was the posthumous son of a history painter, and he trained in the studio of Johann Murrer. From 1688 to 1696 he stayed in Italy, in Rome and Venice among other places. In 1705 he became director of Nuremberg's Academy of Fine Arts. His sequence of works on art theory, Die durch Theorie erfundene Practic, was used as a textbook by students such as Salomon Gessner into the 19th century. Johann Caspar Füssli named him and Jan Kupecky the two most famous Nuremberg artists of the early 18th century. Several of his children became artists.

Joža Uprka painted the folk life of Southern Moravia. He came from a peasant family, and his father was an amateur painter, which inspired Joža and his brother František to take up art. In Munich he was a founder of a Czech student group called Škréta, together with Alfons Mucha and others. In 1888 he went home and began painting scenes of peasant life. In 1904 his house in Hroznová Lhota was rebuilt as a villa designed by Dušan Jurkovič and inspired by folk architecture. It became a meeting place for Czech artists, writers and composers.

For many years Ludwig Koch was a guest at the Spanish Riding School, and he recorded the school jumps in his pictures. He became known mainly as a horse and genre painter. He studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna and won the special school prize for General Pappenheim in 1889. Austrian military history was another subject of his. Even before 1914 he painted portraits and uniforms of the Austro-Hungarian Army, and these were often reproduced on postcards.

Marx Reichlich is described as an Austrian painter who lived from about 1460 to 1520. He painted mostly religious works, many of them commissions for churches. Traditional scenes such as the Adoration of the Magi and the Last Judgement are among them. Some of his works are now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum. His saints include St. Ottilia and St. Mauritius.

People called Maynard Dixon the Last Cowboy in San Francisco. His mother, the daughter of a Navy officer, shared her love of classic literature with him and encouraged his writing and drawing. In 1893 he moved to San Francisco and studied with Arthur Mathews at the California School of Design. In 1900 he visited Arizona and Mexico, and later he made a horseback trip through several western states with the artist Edward Borein. He worked with the cooperative Galerie Beaux Arts to help local modern artists find support. He was married for a time to the photographer Dorothea Lange.

Nathaniel Jocelyn painted William Lloyd Garrison. Garrison called the portrait a tolerable likeness, but he joked that those who imagine he is a monster would deny its accuracy, since it shows no horns. Jocelyn trained as a watchmaker under his father, a clockmaker and engraver, and then took up engraving and oil painting. In 1829 and 1830 he toured Europe with Samuel Morse and the architect Ithiel Town. His 1839 portrait of Joseph Cinqué, leader of a slave revolt, is among his best-known works.

In 1878 the neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot hired Albert Londe as the medical photographer at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris. He stayed about twenty years. He worked alongside Étienne-Jules Marey on photographic experiments with movement, and he modeled his laboratory on Marey's Station Physiologique. In 1882 he devised a system for photographing physical and muscular movements. He was also a pioneer in X-ray photography.

Antoniazzo Romano was fined as a young man for brawling in the streets of Rome. His real name was Antonio di Benedetto Aquilo degli Aquili, and his father was a painter too. He was influenced at first by Benozzo Gozzoli and Beato Angelico. His first recorded work, from 1461, was a copy of the miraculous Virgin and Child of St. Luke in Santa Maria Maggiore. He often repainted older images or made new cult images with an archaic look, using gold grounds that were unusual by his time. He led the Roman school in the later 15th century.

Dirk van Hoogstraten was the father of the painter Samuel van Hoogstraten. His family were Mennonite refugees who left Antwerp for Dordrecht. He was apprenticed to a silversmith and went to Germany to learn the new method of gold- and silver-plating. There he met Dutch painters and turned to drawing and painting instead. Houbraken tells a story about this time. When Dirk fell ill, the woman who let him a room sent for a priest, and he spat out the sacramental bread because he did not want to die a Catholic.

Eelke Jelles Eelkema lost his hearing to an illness at the age of seven, and he was educated at the first Dutch institution for the deaf, in Groningen. Gerardus de San, the first director of the Academie Minerva, taught him to draw. In 1804 he won the academy's first prize. A stipend in 1814 paid for two years in Paris. In 1819 the Haarlem bulb breeder Mattheus van Eeden let him paint the flowers in his Flora nursery, and Eelkema later arranged them as bouquets on canvas at home. He painted landscapes, flowers and fruit.

Around 1200 illustrations for 116 books and 200 separate woodcuts are attributed to Erhard Schön. He was the son of a Nuremberg painter and probably learned his trade in his father's workshop. Dürer was clearly his model, and he may have contributed a few woodcuts to Dürer's Triumphal Arch. Schön made a woodcut portrait of him after he died. He was in demand for popular prints. His first known work is a series of woodcuts for a book from 1513.

Francisco Bayeu was best known for his frescoes. His father made surgical instruments and barbers' tools. He studied first with the local master José Luzán, who had studied with Francesco Solimena in Naples, and he worked as an assistant to Antonio González Velázquez. When he won a scholarship to the Academia de San Fernando in Madrid in 1758, his orphaned siblings followed him. His brothers Ramón and Manuel were also well-known painters.

Thomas Hovenden lost both parents in the Great Famine and was placed in an orphanage at six. He was apprenticed to a carver and gilder and studied at the Cork School of Design. He immigrated to the United States in 1863. In Baltimore he met the collectors William Walters and John McCoy, and McCoy's sponsorship took him to Paris in 1874, where he studied under Cabanel. He painted historical works, domestic scenes and narrative subjects, some showing African Americans.

Valerio Castello was the youngest son of the painter Bernardo Castello, who died when Valerio was six. He and his brothers were attached to the noble Torquato family, and the plan was for him to study a literary profession. His patrons noticed his talent for drawing and arranged an apprenticeship with Domenico Fiasella. Later he studied with Giovanni Andrea de' Ferrari. To seek new inspiration he traveled to Milan and then Parma, probably between 1640 and 1645. In Milan he admired the work of Camillo Procaccini.

Johannes Wilhjelm painted bright, colourful landscapes while travelling in Italy. He came from Nakskov and entered the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in 1888. Later he studied with Krøyer at the Kunstnernes Frie Studieskoler, and in 1903 he spent a year with Kristian Zahrtmann, who had strongly influenced him. He often visited the artists' colony at Skagen in the north of Denmark. There he painted the dunes and beaches. His works also include religious paintings and portraits.

Ambrogio Bergognone worked in and near Milan at nearly the same time as Leonardo da Vinci, but his style is closer to the older Lombard art of Vincenzo Foppa and Bernardino Zenale. The dates of his birth and death are unknown. He is said to have been born in Fossano in Piedmont, and he went by many names, among them Ambrogio da Fossano. His nickname is attributed to his affiliation with the Burgundian school. Only one picture, an altarpiece at the Basilica of Sant'Eustorgio, is a verified example of his work before 1486.

Bartholomeus Barbiers painted landscapes, and he was left-handed. He is also called Bartholomeus Barbiers I, to tell him apart from relatives with the same name. He was born and died in Amsterdam. His father and teacher was Pieter Barbiers, and his brother was Pieter Pietersz Barbiers. His son Pieter Bartholomeusz Barbiers became a painter too. He lived through the change from the Dutch Republic to the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Francesco Tironi painted views of Venice in a Neoclassical style, and he lived from about 1745 to 1797. One of them shows a large crowd in a piazza before the church of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, and another the meeting of Pope Pius VI and the Doge on the island of San Giorgio in Alga. He also made the drawings for Antonio Sandi's twenty-four engravings of 1779, which show islands in the Venetian Lagoon. Many of them show thriving communities on islands that are now desolate.

Ward grew up in Urbana, Ohio, where a neighbor, the potter Miles Chatfield, taught him to throw a pot and decorate it with bas-reliefs. A sculpture exhibition in Cincinnati in 1847 discouraged him, and he turned to medicine until malaria ended his studies. He then trained for seven years under Henry Kirke Brown in Brooklyn. In Washington in 1857 he made a name with portrait busts of public men. His most familiar work is the standing statue of George Washington at Federal Hall in New York.

Marco Zoppo's oldest document, from 1452, shows him at home in Cento, entrusted with the gilding of a statue of the Virgin and Child. The next year he is documented in Padua. Earlier he had been a pupil of Lippo Dalmasio, and for a few years around 1455 he studied with Francesco Squarcione. Andrea Mantegna was a contemporary of his. In Bologna he painted several versions of the Virgin and Child Enthroned with Saints, and Francesco Francia was one of his pupils. He died in Venice in 1498.

Migita Toshihide worked in traditional ukiyo-e prints and also painted in the Western style. He was apprenticed to Tsukioka Yoshitoshi and studied with Kinisawa Shimburō, an artist who had trained in Britain. From 1877 his work was published in newspapers and magazines. His portraits of kabuki actors were well known. One of his pupils, Hirezaki Eihō, later worked as an illustrator for the Asahi Shimbun and became known for his action sketches of sumo bouts.

Simon Du Bois was the youngest son of Hendrick Du Bois, a painter and dealer in works of art. From 1646 to 1653 he lived in Haarlem, where he studied with Berchem and Wouwerman and painted horses and cattle. Then he traveled with his older brother Eduard and began painting small battle scenes in the Italian fashion. He also worked in Venice. From 1685 until his death he worked in England as a portrait painter.

People called Stanhope Forbes the father of the Newlyn School, and he was one of its founding members. He was born in Dublin to a French mother and an English railway manager. His older brother, Sir William Forbes, also worked for the railways. In 1889 he married the painter Elizabeth Armstrong at St Peter's Church in Newlyn. Their first home overlooked the sea. Their son Alexander, known as Alec, was born in 1893.

Thomas Patch was the son of a distinguished doctor and was expected to become an apothecary. He left his medical studies unfinished and went to Rome in 1747 with Richard Dalton, who later became librarian to George III. In Rome he met Joshua Reynolds, who was producing caricature groups at the time. Patch made a living from painting views of Florence and Tivoli. He also sold painted caricature groups to the Anglo-Florentine community and to young British men on the Grand Tour. The largest collection of his work is in the Lewis Walpole Library in Farmington, Connecticut.

Tjipke Visser's work was part of the sculpture event in the art competition at the 1936 Summer Olympics. He was a Dutch sculptor, born in Workum. In 1939 his work was included in the exhibition and sale Onze Kunst van Heden, Our Art of Today, at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. Other records also list him as a painter and draftsperson. He died in 1955.

Virginie Demont-Breton was the daughter of Jules Breton and the niece of Émile Breton, both painters. Her mother, Élodie de Vigne, was a painter and model, and her grandfather was the Flemish painter Félix de Vigne. Rosa Bonheur was her mentor. She finished her first painting at fourteen, and by twenty she was exhibiting at the Salon. In 1880 she married the painter Adrien Demont.

Alois Hans Schram painted much of his work in the Art Nouveau style, though many later works are closer to Neo-Baroque. His father was a councilor for the postal service. He studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna with Carl Wurzinger, Hans Makart and Josef Matyáš Trenkwald. In 1887 he won the Spezialschulpreis for a scene from the life of Bianca Cappello, which is now in the Denver Art Museum. A state scholarship then let him continue his studies in Rome.

Antonio de La Gándara had a father of Spanish ancestry who was born in Mexico, and his mother was English. At fifteen he was admitted to the École des Beaux-Arts as a student of Jean-Léon Gérôme and Cabanel. His first exhibited work, a portrait of Saint Sebastian, was singled out by the jury of the 1883 Salon. Less than ten years later he was one of the favourite artists of the Paris élite. He drew too.

Carl Rasmussen was the eldest of eleven children, and his father was a master tailor who later became City Treasurer. At fifteen he went to Copenhagen to learn the hosiery trade. He was drawn to the art he saw there and took drawing lessons with two architects, and later with the animal painter Didrik Frisch. Short of money, he took passage as a cabin boy on a relative's merchant ship and visited Scotland. He became best known for marine art and scenes of Greenland.

Charles Nègre studied painting with Paul Delaroche, Ingres and Drolling before he took up photography. Delaroche encouraged him to use photographs as research for painting. He started with the daguerreotype and then moved on to calotypes. In 1851 he photographed Chimney-Sweeps Walking on the Quai Bourbon, which may have been a staged study for a painting. It is important to photographic history because it freezes movement in a single moment. He also photographed the Stryge in 1853.

Claude Simpol came from Clamecy and studied under Boullogne and frère Luc. In 1687 he won second prize in the Prix de Rome for Noah's Flood. He specialised in grisailles. The Académie royale admitted him in 1701, but in 1709 he was still listed as not having handed in his academy piece, Neptune's Dispute with Minerva. Pierre-Jean Mariette described him as an artist with little love for work.

Dwight William Tryon taught himself from the art instruction manuals on the shelves of a Hartford bookstore where he worked as a young man. His father was killed in a gun accident before Tryon turned four, and his mother raised him on his grandparents' farm in East Hartford. He sketched in his off hours. He sold his first painting in 1870. Influenced by James McNeill Whistler, he is best known for landscapes and seascapes in a tonalist style.

Edouard Agneessens studied under Jean-François Portaels at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels and won the Prix de Rome in 1869. A year earlier he had been a founding member of the Société Libre des Beaux-Arts. He built up a career in Saint-Petersburg but returned to Brussels in the 1880s. In the last part of his life he suffered from a mental disorder. He died in 1885 in Uccle.

Elisabeth Barbara Schmetterling learned art from her father, a miniaturist, in Amsterdam, where she was born and grew up. She began with printmaking and showed her prints at the Exhibitions of Living Masters. She also made illustrations for children's books and for an almanac, the Nederlandsche Muzen-Almanak. Around 1830 she turned to miniatures, doing portraits and copies after 17th-century masters. She died in Amsterdam at 80. The Rijksmuseum has her work.

Kanō Hōgai was the son of the chief painter to the local daimyo. He went to Edo in 1846 and spent ten years at the Kobikichō studio under Kanō Shōsen'in. After the Meiji restoration ended the old patronage system, he struggled with money in the 1870s and took up iron casting and land reclamation. He came back through government-sponsored exhibitions. His style joined Kanō brush painting with Western ideas of linear and aerial perspective. Hibo Kannon, which shows the bodhisattva Kannon standing on a cloud, is one of his most notable works.

Vicente Palmaroli took over his father's official post at the royal art collections after his father died. Four years later he asked for leave to go to Rome, using surplus money from the collection fund. There he joined Spanish painters who met at the Antico Caffè Greco. In 1873 he settled in Paris and specialized in tableautins, small paintings on amusing or pleasant themes for the home. In 1894 he was appointed Director of the Museo del Prado and held the post until his death. He died in 1896.

Isabella Ruth Doerfler worked for the Federal Arts Project in the 1930s and was called one of the best renderers of textiles in New England. She graduated from the Yale School of Art in 1909. Over the years she taught school, illustrated children's books, decorated antiques and designed for publishing houses. In 1936 she contributed to the Index of American Design. During World War II she worked in the mechanical drawing department of a defense factory. The National Gallery of Art holds twenty of her watercolors.

Alfred-Alexandre Delauney came to Paris at twelve to work as an assistant to his uncle Salmon, a print seller with a shop called Librairie des Beaux-Arts on the Rue de Seine. The shop passed to Delauney in 1850. He etched paintings by Jean-François Millet, and his etching L'Hiver aux corbeaux has been noted as an inspiration to Vincent van Gogh. Twenty-four of his etchings were published as Eaux-Fortes sur le vieux Paris. He married Elise Varin, the daughter of the engraver Pierre-Amédée Varin.

Jean-Laurent Mosnier served as a court painter under the Ancien Régime, and from 1789 he worked as a society painter in London, Hamburg and St. Petersburg. His self-portrait with his young daughters is thought to copy the success of Adélaïde Labille-Guiard's Self-Portrait with Two Pupils. It is in the Hermitage. For his reception into the Académie Royale in 1788 he painted portraits of Charles-Antoine Bridan and Louis-Jean-François Lagrenée. He is best known for portraits. He worked in miniature as well as on easel paintings.
